# Beyond Being Right

[Silas Bambil · December 2025]{.meta}

I have always enjoyed the satisfaction of arriving at the correct answer to a difficult mathematical problem. I have been academically bright for as long as I can remember, learnt quickly, and generally performed well in school. Being intelligent was something I valued about myself, and it gradually became an important part of my identity. What I did not realise for a long time was how little my ability to understand complicated academic concepts told me about my ability to understand other people. In mathematics, I knew when I had insufficient information to solve a problem. I was not always so careful when forming opinions about people.

Being accustomed to understanding things quickly influenced the expectations I developed of others. When someone struggled to understand something I found relatively straightforward, I did not always appreciate why they needed more time. I sometimes mistook difficulty for insufficient effort, without considering that the ease with which I understood something might have made me less able to appreciate someone else's struggles with it. Looking back, I find it somewhat ironic that an ability I considered one of my greatest strengths occasionally prevented me from recognising the limitations of my own understanding.

I was quick to judge, quick to dismiss, and often too slow to listen. These are not particularly flattering things to acknowledge about oneself, especially when one has spent much of one's life taking pride in being knowledgeable. Some of what I previously regarded as intellectual confidence was, in retrospect, impatience. The difficulty with becoming accustomed to being right is that we may gradually become less interested in discovering whether we are wrong. When being intelligent becomes an important part of one's identity, even an ordinary disagreement can begin to feel like something more personal than it ought to be.

I remain fascinated by mathematics, statistics, and the many things that formal education enables us to understand. But reading another textbook will not necessarily help me understand why someone finds a particular situation frightening, why they respond differently to disappointment, or why something I consider insignificant matters deeply to them. Other people possess knowledge acquired through experiences I may never have. Some of that knowledge cannot be obtained by studying harder or becoming more accomplished academically. It requires a willingness to take an interest in lives that have developed quite differently from one's own.

I have also learnt to distinguish more carefully between disagreeing with someone and forming an opinion about their intelligence. A person can express an incorrect opinion without being unintelligent, just as someone can arrive at a correct conclusion without having understood the subject particularly well. I still believe that arguments should be evaluated according to evidence and sound reasoning. However, there is little reason for a disagreement about an idea to become an assessment of someone's worth. Sometimes, understanding why a person holds a particular view proves more interesting than establishing why I disagree with it.

Listening becomes a rather different activity when we are genuinely interested in discovering something. If I spend most of a conversation looking for weaknesses in what someone is saying, I may leave it knowing little more about the person than I did when it began. I have grown to appreciate conversations in which neither person changes their position, but both leave with a better understanding of each other. Not every worthwhile discussion needs to end with someone conceding a point. Sometimes, discovering why a reasonable person sees things differently is itself a worthwhile intellectual exercise.

It would be rather convenient if the abilities I possessed were also the most important abilities a person could possess. An academically successful individual might place enormous value on formal education, while someone who communicates confidently might underestimate quieter people. We sometimes develop standards of competence that place us rather favourably among those we evaluate. Yet someone who struggles with mathematics may possess practical judgement, patience, or an understanding of human relationships that I have yet to develop. Recognising such qualities in other people does not require me to think any less of my own abilities.

As I have grown older, I have become more aware of how much people's circumstances influence their lives. We often encounter someone at a particular point in their life and reach conclusions that extend well beyond what that encounter can reasonably support. We know what they do for a living, where they went to school, or what they have accomplished. We rarely know as much about the opportunities they had, the responsibilities they carried, or the difficulties they encountered. I find it curious that we can be so demanding about the quality of information we use in our academic work and so easily satisfied with the little we know about other people.

I believe in hard work, discipline, and personal responsibility. Nevertheless, effort does not always manifest itself as success. One person may devote considerable energy to advancing their career, while another works equally hard simply to maintain a degree of financial stability. The former may have several accomplishments to point to at the end of the year; the latter may have little more to show than the fact that their circumstances did not deteriorate. It would be difficult to appreciate what that second person has accomplished without first understanding what it took for them to remain where they were.

We are generally quite familiar with the sacrifices that went into our own achievements. We remember the difficult periods, the hours we spent working, and the things we had to do without. What we may remember less readily are the advantages that allowed those efforts to produce favourable outcomes. A good education, supportive relationships, reasonably good health, and access to opportunities can influence what becomes possible through hard work. Acknowledging these advantages does not make our achievements any less deserving of recognition. Success deserves celebration, but it provides a rather incomplete basis for judging the character of those who have been less fortunate.

I have also become more cautious about interpreting people's behaviour when they appear to be struggling. Someone who seems distracted may have responsibilities that occupy much of their attention. A colleague whose performance has deteriorated may be dealing with something they would rather not discuss. Even among people we consider close friends, there may be difficulties of which we are entirely unaware. Certainly, not everyone is doing their best at every moment. But I am less inclined than I once was to assume that someone is making little effort simply because I cannot see much evidence of progress.

People at the lowest points of their fortunes deserve the most grace, not judgement. Unfortunately, those are often the very points at which understanding becomes hardest to obtain. When someone is successful, their confidence may be regarded as an admirable quality, their mistakes overlooked, and their shortcomings interpreted generously. Should their fortunes decline, the same qualities may suddenly become less tolerable to the people around them. Whatever difficulties a person is already experiencing, having to establish that they remain worthy of other people's consideration should not become an additional burden.

A person's dignity should not fluctuate with their fortunes. Losing one's job does not make one less deserving of respect than one was while employed. A student who consistently struggles deserves no less patience than the student whose academic performance inspires admiration. I am increasingly interested in how we treat people whose positions offer us little personal advantage. Respecting someone because of their accomplishments is relatively easy. What is more revealing is whether our regard for that person would remain if the accomplishments, the professional title, or the favourable financial circumstances were no longer there.

Our own circumstances also warrant a little humility. Someone who feels particularly competent in one environment may find themselves inexperienced in another. A person who enjoys financial security may never have encountered the conditions that make financial stability so difficult for someone else to attain. We cannot always distinguish between the things we are capable of overcoming and the things we have simply been fortunate enough not to face. I would rather be grateful for the circumstances that have favoured me than regard them as permanent evidence of my superiority over people whose lives have been different.

To me, extending grace means allowing people a little room to be human without immediately forming lasting opinions about them. Someone may need more time to understand something, another opportunity to correct a mistake, or simply enough patience to explain themselves properly. There is a certain comfort in knowing that one can admit to struggling without immediately becoming the subject of ridicule or disappointment. I would like the people around me to experience that comfort. A person should be able to acknowledge a limitation without having to worry that it will become the defining feature of how others regard them.

Extending grace does not, however, require abandoning accountability. Some arguments are incorrect, some decisions are irresponsible, and some behaviour is unacceptable. Understanding why someone behaved in a particular way does not necessarily justify their behaviour. Nevertheless, the manner in which we address people's shortcomings remains within our control. Someone can be corrected without being humiliated and held responsible without being made to feel worthless. I see little value in responding to a mistake in a way that makes the person who committed it increasingly reluctant to acknowledge another one.

The same principle applies to how I want to use my intelligence. If I understand something well, that knowledge should put me in a better position to help someone who does not. Making that person feel unintelligent contributes nothing to the quality of my explanation. They may eventually forget the details of what I explained but remember whether they felt comfortable asking me a question. I would like my knowledge to make it easier for other people to learn, rather than make them increasingly reluctant to reveal the things they do not know.

I have also grown more comfortable with discovering that I am wrong. After all, if the purpose of acquiring knowledge is to improve my understanding, it would be rather strange to resent discovering an opportunity to do precisely that. There is no need to defend an opinion indefinitely simply because it was once mine. I still enjoy intellectual discussions and believe in defending conclusions supported by good evidence. But I would much rather leave a conversation having learnt something than leave it with the satisfaction of having defended a position I ought to have reconsidered.

None of this means that I have become an exceptionally patient or understanding person. I still experience frustration, occasionally form premature impressions, and sometimes need to reconsider how I respond to others. Becoming aware of one's shortcomings does not automatically eliminate them. What I have gained is a greater willingness to question my immediate reactions, whether I am dealing with a friend's mistake, a colleague's difficulties, or someone whose choices I do not understand. Occasionally, the most reasonable thing I can do is acknowledge that I have not yet given the person sufficient consideration to justify the opinion I have formed.

I remain grateful for my intelligence and for the opportunities I have had to develop it. I still enjoy learning difficult things, challenging ideas, and discovering weaknesses in my own understanding. Growing older has given me a wider appreciation of what there is to understand, particularly about people whose lives differ from mine. I did not lose intelligence or conviction in the process. I gained perspective. For much of my life, I took pride in how quickly I could arrive at an answer. I have since learnt that, when it comes to understanding people, there are occasions when the more intelligent thing to do is to give myself a little longer before reaching one.
